sections.title: The Mitzva of Health and the Prohibition of Dangerous Foods
sections.html:
It is forbidden to eat foods that may contain poisons, and even when the concern about this is remote, it is forbidden to eat them. For the Sages learned that a person must be very careful to guard his life, as it is stated (Devarim 4:9): “Only take heed to yourself, and guard your soul diligently,” and it is stated (ibid. 15): “Take therefore good heed to yourselves.” True, these verses were said as a warning concerning faith in God, His Torah and His mitzvot, which are the purpose of the existence of a person's soul. However, the first condition for the fulfillment of faith is that a person lives and does not die, and therefore these verses also obligate a person to guard his life from death and from illness. As the Rambam wrote (Hilkhot De'ot 4:1): “Since keeping the body healthy and whole is among the ways of God, for it is impossible to understand or know anything while one is ill, a person must distance himself from things that destroy the body, and accustom himself to things that make him healthy and strong.” Even when the concern of danger to life is remote, the Sages ruled that one must be more stringent about it than about a concern of prohibition, for ḥamira sakkanta me-issura – “danger is more severe than prohibition” (Ḥullin 10a; Rema 116:5). And one who endangers himself by eating something dangerous and dies will be held to account for it, as it is stated (Bereishit 9:5): “And surely your blood of your lives will I require.”

Eating foods that harm the body's health is also forbidden, and one who guards his health fulfills a mitzva, and this is included in what the Torah instructed (Devarim 28:9): “And you shall walk in His ways.” For God created our bodies to be healthy, and we must guard them and not eat foods that will impair their health. Moreover, good health enables a person to engage in Torah study and to fulfill the mitzvot with joy. Accordingly, the great Torah scholars of every generation used to guide their students in the ways of health, as explained in the Talmud and in the books of the poskim and of musar. And if even destroying food is forbidden, all the more so it is forbidden for a person to destroy his body by harming his health (Shabbat 140b).

In all medical guidance we must follow what is accepted by the physicians of our generation. In practice, the guidance accepted today is to reduce as much as possible the eating of processed foods, and of foods high in sugar, margarine, salt, white flour, and saturated and trans fat. Among the foods characterized by these ingredients are soft drinks, industrial snacks, sausages, bourekas and cakes. On the other hand, it is recommended to eat plenty of vegetables and fruit and to drink water. And above all, not to eat too much, and to make sure to get physical activity and good sleep. However, one must also beware of drastic diets and extreme health practices, since joy and naturalness are the foundation of health, and excessive caution and strictness harm them (see Peninei Halakha, Berakhot 13:9-11).1

sections.title: The Prohibition of Uncovered Liquids Due to the Danger of Venom
sections.html:
In the past, venomous snakes were common in the vicinity of houses, and sometimes they would discharge venom into water, wine or milk, and sometimes they would peck at fruits and foods, and one who drank from those liquids or ate from those foods could die. Therefore, the Sages forbade drinking and using liquids that had been left uncovered, and forbade eating fruits and foods that have signs of pecking. Not only that, but they ruled that if wine of teruma was left uncovered for a length of time in which a snake could come out of a nearby place and drink from it, the wine must be poured out. And although it is forbidden to destroy teruma, because it has been sanctified for eating by kohanim, because of the concern of danger they ruled that it be destroyed (Mishna Terumot 8:4-7).

However, already in the days of the Rishonim, snakes were not common in the vicinity of houses, and the Rishonim ruled that it is permitted to drink liquids that had been left uncovered, because the prohibition was instituted for a place where snakes are common, and when they are not present, the prohibition lapses (Tosafot Avoda Zara 35a, s.v. “Ḥada”; Rosh, Rashba, SA 116:1). Therefore, it is permitted to leave water and other liquids uncovered, and it is permitted le-khatḥila to drink them. Only if one actually sees a snake or other venomous creatures drinking from the liquid is it forbidden to drink it (Levush 116:1). However, one does not recite Kiddush over wine that was left uncovered for several hours, for since it would be shameful to serve it to a distinguished person, all the more so one should not fulfill the mitzva of Kiddush over it (SA OḤ 272:1). Some are scrupulous even nowadays to cover water and other liquids, out of respect for the prohibition that the Sages instituted, which perhaps has additional reasons. And also for the sake of cleanliness, so that creeping creatures and dirt do not get into them (Shelah, the Gra).

sections.title: Health Warnings
sections.html:
The Sages warned that a person should not put a coin in his mouth, lest a sick person touched it and he catch his illness. They also warned against swallowing human sweat, and that sweat should not get mixed into cooked dishes. They also warned that a person should not place bread under his armpit, lest sweat stick to it (Yerushalmi Terumot 8:3; SA 116:4-5).

Likewise, people who prepare food must be careful about the cleanliness of their hands. In particular, cooks who prepare food for the public must make sure to wash their hands and fingers well with water and soap before they touch the food. And every time they go out to relieve themselves, when they return they should wash their hands with water and soap. Likewise, when the cook is ill with a contagious disease, he must refrain from preparing food, so that he does not infect those who eat with his illness.

One must be especially careful when preparing foods from animals, since bacteria and contaminants are more commonly found in them. Therefore, one who handles meat or fish before cooking must immediately afterwards wash his hands with water and soap in order to disinfect them of bacteria and contaminants. For cooking eliminates the bacteria and contaminants in the meat and fish, but not what remains on the hands of the person who touched them before cooking. Likewise, it is proper to wash well with water and soap surfaces on which raw meat and fish were cut, in order to prevent bacteria from passing to other foods.

One must make sure to keep cooked dishes in the refrigerator, because in warm conditions bacteria multiply in them that can cause food poisoning. When one takes a liquid dish out of the refrigerator and wishes to heat it, one must make sure to heat it until it steams, in order to disinfect it of bacteria that may develop in it during the heating. Above all, one must be careful to keep well refrigerated foods from animals that have not been cooked, such as foods that contain raw eggs, like mayonnaise, in which dangerous bacteria such as salmonella and E. coli may develop.

Likewise, one must be careful not to place a knife in a manner that could endanger people. For example, one should not stick a knife into a fruit, lest a person not notice the knife, and when he leans on the fruit or falls on it, he will be injured (Yerushalmi Terumot 8:3; Rambam, Hilkhot Rotze'aḥ 12:6; SA 116:5).

sections.title: Meat and Fish Together
sections.html:
The Jewish people have been accustomed not to eat meat with fish, because there was a medical position that eating them together can cause tzara'at (a skin disease) and bad breath (Pesaḥim 76b; SA 116:2). However, from many Rishonim it is implied that there is no prohibition in this, and from the Rambam it emerges explicitly that it is permitted to eat fish that was roasted with meat (Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Assurot 9:23). The poskim explained that from his studies and experience as a physician he concluded that there is no danger in this, and consequently there is no prohibition against eating fish and meat together. However, the overwhelming majority of the Aḥaronim were concerned about the danger in this, and although the physicians of their time did not warn against eating meat and fish, on the other hand they also could not guarantee that eating them involves no danger. For the opinion of physicians rested on estimates, tradition and personal experience, and consequently the attitude to the physicians' position was that one should take it into account but not accept it with certainty. Consequently, they could not rely on them to cancel the concern of danger in eating fish and meat. Therefore, only in cases of doubt did the Aḥaronim add the Rambam's opinion as a basis for leniency (Ḥatam Sofer YD 101; Divrei Malkiel 2:53).

However, today, when medical science rests on systematic research that is examined in various places around the world, with exchange of information among all the research and medical centers, medical positions are considered more well-founded. Consequently, since all physicians in our day agree that there is no danger in eating fish with meat, and this was also the opinion of some of the poskim, there is no prohibition in it. And one should not claim that this is a violation of the words of the Sages, because in medical matters the Sages did not have a halakhic position; rather, based on the mitzva to guard one's health, they guided the public to follow the medical instructions accepted in their time. Today, when it is clear to physicians that there is no danger in this, there is no prohibition in it.

However, since for generations the Jewish people have been accustomed not to eat meat and fish together, to the point that separating them is one of the distinguishing features of the Jewish kitchen and its etiquette, the accepted custom is to be careful not to cook meat with fish, and not to serve meat and fish on one plate. When one wishes to eat a fish course and a meat course, one prepares a separate fork, knife and plate for each course. When necessary, one wipes them with a napkin or with bread before eating the second kind, or cleans the fork and knife with one's mouth, so that remnants of one kind do not get mixed with the other kind. If gravy from one kind remains on one's fingers, one washes them or wipes them with a napkin. Likewise, one drinks something between eating them (SA and Rema 116:3; Pri To'ar 4).2

sections.title: Fish with Milk
sections.html:
It is permitted to cook fish with milk, and it is likewise permitted to eat fish with milk. For the Sages did not decree that fish be regarded as meat, since their appearance is very different, and their law is also different, for they do not require sheḥita and their blood is permitted to eat. So it is explained in the Mishna (Ḥullin 103b), that it is permitted to cook and eat fish with milk, and so it is explained in the Talmud (ibid. 111b), that people used to dip fish in a dairy sauce.

However, Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote (Beit Yosef YD 87:3) that one should not eat fish with milk because of a concern of danger, and following his words, in the lands of the East and North Africa, many were accustomed to be careful about this. Some said that one need be careful only about eating fish with milk, but not about eating them with butter (Zivḥei Tzedek). On the other hand, among the Sephardic poskim too, there were some who permitted eating fish with milk (Pri Ḥadash, Ḥida, Shulḥan Gavo'ah).

In practice, today members of all communities are permitted to eat fish with milk, since it is explained in the Talmud and the Rishonim that eating them together is permitted le-khatḥila. Even those who were accustomed to be stringent were stringent for a medical reason only, and since physicians in our day agree that there is no danger in this, the prohibition has lapsed. It is possible that in the past, in certain regions, bacteria were present in milk which, upon meeting fish, became active and caused illnesses, and from experience, the physicians in those places instructed people to avoid eating fish with milk. And since it is a mitzva to beware of dangers, the rabbis in those places ruled that people should listen to them. But today, when the custom is to pasteurize milk, there is no longer any need to be concerned about those illnesses, and even those who were stringent about this in the past may eat fish with milk.3

sections.title: The Attitude toward Concern for Supernatural Dangers
sections.html:
Nowadays there is no need to be concerned about precautionary customs that the ancients practiced because of the concern of segula (supernatural) dangers, that is, dangers stemming from evil spirits and demons. We learn this from the custom of being careful about zugot (“pairs”) (Pesaḥim 110a): in the times of the Talmud many were careful not to drink cups or eat foods in an even number, so as not to be harmed by demons. Therefore they were careful to drink one cup, or three or five, and not two or four or six and so on, and likewise with foods such as eggs. One can explain that these demons received their power from the religion of the Magi (of Zoroaster), which believes that there are two forces in the world, good and evil, and those who ate or drank in pairs were harmed by demons and spirits of this idolatry. However, the Sages added and stated a rule (Pesaḥim 110b): “Kol de-kapid – kapdei bahadei, ve-dela kapid – la kapdei bahadei. U-miho le-meiḥash mibaei.” Translation: “Whoever is particular – they are particular with him; and whoever is not particular – they are not particular with him. However, one should be concerned.” That is, one who is particular to beware of these dangers and did not take care may be harmed, and one who is not particular and drank in pairs – those demons and evil spirits do not harm him; however, le-khatḥila it is better that he not expose himself to their danger and not drink in pairs, for sometimes they harm even one who is not concerned about them.

The explanation is that the spiritual worlds are composed of different worlds and dimensions. In each world there are good and beneficial forces, and evil and harmful ones. In worlds that tend toward the imagination and mysticism, these forces appear as angels, spirits and demons that have a presence that influences for good and for bad, each world according to the type of imaginative consciousness within it. And in worlds that tend toward the intellect, they appear as good and bad ideas that spread and influence the individual and humanity, each world according to the conceptions that lie at its foundation.

Every person has his own world of consciousness, and in the world where his consciousness is, there he lives, and the forces that act in that world influence him for good and for bad. This is what the Sages said: “Whoever is particular – they are particular with him; and whoever is not particular – they are not particular with him.” That is, one whose consciousness is in a world of certain spirits and demons, such as those that harm people who drink in pairs, is influenced by their activity. And one whose consciousness is not there – those demons do not act upon him. Nevertheless, the Sages said that it is proper for him to be concerned about things known to be dangerous. For although his consciousness is far from these demons and spirits, since he lives in a period in which awareness of them is widespread, and he himself is concerned about demons and spirits of a different kind, inevitably the demons and spirits that harm those who drink in pairs also have a certain influence on him, and therefore it is proper for him to beware of their danger. However, today, when almost all of the Jewish people live in a consciousness of intellectual spiritual worlds, in which there is no place for demons and spirits, and even the hidden teachings of the Torah and the rich worlds of the imagination are explained rationally, it is not proper to be concerned about the danger of harmful spirits. Only those people who still give them a place in their worldview, because of their inclination or their upbringing, need to be concerned about them.4

sections.title: Supernatural Warnings for Those Who Are Particular
sections.html:
Based on the principles we have learned, let us explain the attitude toward various precautionary customs. Some are accustomed not to eat peeled garlic, a peeled onion or a peeled egg that was left overnight, even if they were closed inside a vessel or wrapped in a bag, because of the concern of an evil spirit. However, many are not accustomed to be concerned about this, because this warning was not codified as halakha in the Rambam, in most of the books of the Rishonim, or in the Shulḥan Arukh. And even if in the times of the Tanna'im that evil spirit could cause harm, over time the concern about it lapsed. And so is the halakha: it is not proper to institute prohibitions that have no root in halakha and whose reason is based on a danger that is not discernible in our days. However, one whose family was accustomed to be concerned about this, and who mistakenly left them uncovered overnight, may refrain from eating them without being concerned about the prohibition of bal tashḥit.5

From the period of the Geonim, there were those who took care not to drink water at the she'at ha-tekufa (the hour of the season's change). The solar year is divided into four parts, and the she'at ha-tekufa is the moment at which the seasons change. Some were accustomed to refrain from drinking water that stood drawn at that hour, unless they placed iron in it (Rema YD 116:5; OḤ 455:1). On the other hand, the opinion of Geonim and Rishonim is that it is not proper to be concerned about this at all (Rav Hai Gaon, Ibn Ezra). And so is the custom in practice.6

The Sages warned not to drink water at night from rivers and lakes, for since one cannot see what is in the water, there is a concern that one may swallow a leech (Avoda Zara 12b). But concerns related to demons and spirits are not taken into account.7

sections.title: Supernatural Warnings That Have Additional Reasons
sections.html:
There are warnings that also have moral reasons, and it is proper to heed them, for sometimes the supernatural danger corresponds to the depth of the moral reason. For example, the Sages said that it is proper to be careful not to throw bread crumbs on the floor, for one who does so causes himself poverty, since the angel appointed over food and livelihood is named Nakid, that is, his name is “Cleanliness,” whereas the angel appointed over poverty is named Naval, that is, his name is “Dirt.” Therefore, in a place where there are food crumbs on the floor, the angel of poverty dwells, whereas in a clean place the angel of wealth dwells (Pesaḥim 111b; Ḥullin 105b; SA OḤ 180:4). It is proper to be careful about this, because this supernatural guidance corresponds to the moral guidance, for one who throws crumbs on the ground appears to be kicking at God's blessing, and it is fitting that the blessing should cease for him. Furthermore, neglecting the cleanliness of the home accustoms one to neglect in other areas as well, including the management of money and property, and consequently it causes poverty (above 13:12).

Many are accustomed not to place cooked foods and drinks under the bed, since foods placed there may become dirty or be forgotten and become moldy. Furthermore, sleep is considered one-sixtieth of death, and it is not fitting for the dignity of foods, which are meant to give vitality, to be under the bed on which a person lies motionless like a dead person. Some are even concerned about an evil spirit that rests upon foods that were under the bed during sleep, and therefore they refrain from eating foods and drinks that were under the bed. In practice, le-khatḥila one should not place foods and drinks under the bed, and if one did place them there, it is permitted to eat them.8
